faq.a: Yes; renal, neuro, or hematologic manifestations may be the first signs.
faq.q: Can SLE present without a rash?

faq.a: No; anti‑centromere or anti‑Scl‑70 antibodies are more specific.
faq.q: Is a normal ANA enough to rule out systemic sclerosis?

faq.a: Acetaminophen; avoid NSAIDs which can worsen renal function.
faq.q: What is the safest analgesic for an SLE patient with renal disease?

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman with malar rash, arthritis and 2+ proteinuria – what is the next diagnostic step? — Order ANA and anti‑dsDNA; a positive result confirms SLE and guides treatment.
A tall 30‑year‑old man with aortic root dilation on bedside ultrasound – which medication reduces his risk of dissection? — Beta‑blocker; it lowers shear stress on the aortic wall.

A patient with hyper‑extensible skin and joint dislocations presents after a minor fall – which investigation confirms the diagnosis? — Beighton scoring plus skin biopsy for collagen abnormality; confirms Ehlers‑Danlos.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a patient has positive ANA but no other SLE features – how do you interpret? — Consider false‑positive ANA from infection; repeat testing after malaria treatment before labeling SLE.
A pregnant woman with known SLE needs disease control – which drug is preferred and why? — Hydroxychloroquine; safe in pregnancy and reduces flare risk.
A child with systemic sclerosis shows tightening skin and dysphagia – what complication should you monitor urgently? — Pulmonary fibrosis; obtain chest X‑ray or ultrasound if CT unavailable.

A patient on long‑term steroids for lupus develops new hypertension and bruising – what is the likely cause and management? — Steroid‑induced Cushingoid changes; taper steroids and start antihypertensive if needed.

You suspect lupus nephritis but have no access to renal biopsy – what bedside test helps assess severity? — Urine protein dipstick and serum creatinine; heavy proteinuria (>1 g/day) indicates severe disease.
ai.title: Connective Tissue Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Connective tissue disorders affect the structural framework of organs, leading to multisystem disease. Recognise patterns, use limited investigations, and manage complications in low‑resource settings.

b: Three main groups: hereditary (e.g., Marfan, Ehlers‑Danlos), autoimmune (systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis), and metabolic (amyloidosis, diabetes‑related).
In low‑resource East African hospitals, SLE, systemic sclerosis and Ehlers‑Danlos are the common presentations.
sections.p: Connective tissue provides support, elasticity and repair. Disorders arise from genetic defects, autoimmune attack or metabolic injury, causing skin, joint, vascular and organ manifestations.

b: Autoimmune CTD: ANA positive, multi‑organ involvement, often triggered by infections (TB, HIV).
Hereditary CTD: family history, tall habitus (Marfan), hyper‑extensible skin (Ehlers‑Danlos).
sections.p: Identify the organ systems involved, recognise characteristic skin or joint signs, and apply simple criteria to differentiate autoimmune from hereditary disease.

b: Look for malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers → suspect SLE.
Check for arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, lens subluxation → suspect Marfan.
sections.p: Patients may present with joint pain, skin changes, or organ dysfunction. Early recognition prevents irreversible damage such as renal failure in lupus or aortic dissection in Marfan.

t.b: Is an autoimmune process present? Positive ANA supports SLE or systemic sclerosis; negative does not rule out disease.
Specific for SLE; high titres correlate with renal involvement.
Detects aortic root dilation in Marfan; if unavailable, assess pulse deficits and blood pressure discrepancy between arms.
Confirms Ehlers‑Danlos or cutaneous amyloidosis when histology is needed.
Screens for lupus nephritis; ≥1+ protein warrants further evaluation.

b: SLE: hydroxychloroquine (disease‑modifying, safe in pregnancy) plus steroids for flares; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment.
Marfan: beta‑blocker to reduce aortic wall stress; refer for surgical repair if aortic diameter >5 cm.
Ehlers‑Danlos: physiotherapy, joint protection, avoid invasive procedures that may cause poor wound healing.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect vulnerable organs and provide symptomatic relief.

b: Rheumatoid arthritis – symmetric small‑joint erosions, no systemic skin signs.
Infective endocarditis – fever and murmur but negative ANA and positive blood cultures.
sections.p: Distinguish CTD from isolated rheumatic disease or infection‑related arthropathy.

b: Malaria can cause false‑positive ANA; interpret with clinical picture.
Proteinuria from dehydration may mimic lupus nephritis; repeat testing after rehydration.
sections.p: Autoantibodies may be transiently positive in infections; a normal ANA does not exclude SLE if clinical criteria are met.

b: Use the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria for SLE – need ≥10 points from clinical and immunologic domains.
Apply the Ghent criteria for Marfan – aortic root >2 SD above mean or Z‑score > 2.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition and limited bedside tools.

b: Treating mild joint pain with high‑dose steroids without confirming autoimmune disease.
Missing aortic dilation because echocardiography is unavailable; use clinical clues.
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on single tests and ignore resource constraints.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain or dyspnoea (possible aortic dissection in Marfan).
Rapidly rising creatinine or heavy proteinuria (lupus nephritis flare).
Severe skin ulceration with systemic signs (possible vasculitis).
